stimuli.text: A block of mass 6 kg on a 37° incline is connected by a light string over a light, frictionless pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block of mass 7 kg. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is 0.25. The system is released from rest, and the hanging block descends.
A block of mass 0.3 kg on a horizontal frictionless surface is attached to a spring. Its position is $$x(t) = 0.07\cos(5t)$$, with x in meters and t in seconds.
Students measure the period of a simple pendulum for several string lengths, using small amplitudes.
A solid sphere (I = ⅖MR²) and a solid cylinder (I = ½MR²) of equal mass M and radius R are released from rest at the top of the same ramp of height 1.3 m. Both roll without slipping.

questions.stem: An oscillator's position is $$x(t) = 0.12\cos(13t)$$ m. What is its maximum speed?

options.why: Multiply by ω.
That is a_max.
v_max = Aω.
Correct. v_max = Aω.

questions.stem: A wheel spinning at 35 rad/s slows uniformly to rest in 14 s. How many revolutions does it make while stopping?

options.why: The average angular speed is ω₀/2.
That is in radians; convert to revolutions.
Correct. Δθ = ½ω₀t, then divide by 2π.
Recheck the average.

questions.stem: A cart moving at 6 m/s accelerates uniformly at 3 m/s² over 14 m. What is its final speed?

options.why: Correct. Use v² = v₀² + 2aΔx.
The equation has 2aΔx.
Take the square root.
Square roots do not add term by term.

questions.stem: A planet has 3 times Earth's mass and 2 times Earth's radius. What is the gravitational field strength at its surface? (Earth's is 9.8 N/kg.)

options.why: g decreases with radius.
g depends on 1/R², not 1/R.
The ratio is inverted.
Correct. g ∝ M/R².

questions.stem: A spring with $$k = 430$$ N/m is compressed 0.25 m and launches a 0.6 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed after leaving the spring?

options.why: Take the square root.
Correct. ½kx² = ½mv².
Use energy: v = x√(k/m).
The ½ appears on both sides.

questions.stem: A motor lifts a 140 kg load 20 m at constant speed in 7 s. What average power does it deliver?

options.why: That is the work; divide by time.
P = W/t.
Correct. P = mgh/t.
Include g.

questions.stem: A 8 kg cart moving at 8 m/s collides with and sticks to a 2 kg cart at rest. What is their speed after the collision?

options.why: Use m₁v₁ for the initial momentum.
Correct. Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.
Kinetic energy is not conserved here.
The carts share the momentum.

questions.explanation: v_f = 8·8/10 = 6.4 m/s; kinetic energy lost = 51.2 J.

questions.stem: A 71 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator that is accelerating downward at 2 m/s². What does the scale read?

options.why: Include gravity.
Correct. The scale reads the normal force: N − mg = ma (up positive).
The acceleration changes the normal force.
Check the direction of the acceleration.

questions.stem: A 0.9 kg ball hits a wall at 16 m/s and rebounds at 7 m/s. The contact lasts 0.03 s. What is the average force from the wall?

options.why: Divide by time.
The velocity reverses, so the speeds add.
Correct. Δp = m(v_f − v_i) with the direction reversed.
Include the rebound.

questions.stem: A boat points straight across a river 180 m wide, moving at 6 m/s relative to the water. The current flows at 2 m/s. How long does the crossing take?

options.why: The current is perpendicular to the heading.
The current is perpendicular to the heading.
The perpendicular component alone sets the crossing time.
Correct. The current does not change the time to cross; it only carries the boat downstream.

questions.stem: A 0.9 kg mass oscillates on a spring with $$k = 35$$ N/m. What is the period?

options.why: That is the frequency.
The ratio is m/k.
Include the 2π.
Correct. T = 2π√(m/k).

questions.stem: A particle's position is $$x(t) = -2t^3 + 5t^2 - 6t$$, with x in meters and t in seconds. What is its velocity at $$t = 3$$ s?

options.why: The constant term c is part of the velocity.
Bring each exponent down as a factor when differentiating.
That is the position; differentiate it.
Correct. Differentiate once: v = 3at² + 2bt + c.

questions.explanation: v(t) = -6t² + 10t - 6, so at t = 3 the value is -30.

questions.stem: Masses of 9 kg and 2 kg hang on either side of a light, frictionless pulley. What is the tension in the string?

options.why: Correct. T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).
Use T = m₂(g + a).
The lighter mass accelerates up, so T exceeds its weight.
The heavier mass accelerates down, so T is less than its weight.

questions.stem: A thin spherical shell rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of height 2.9 m. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Rotational energy is ½Iω² = ½βmv².
Some energy goes into rotation.
Correct. mgh = ½mv²(1 + β) with I = ⅔MR².
That is only correct for a hoop.

questions.stem: A 5 kg block on a horizontal table is connected by a string over a light pulley to a hanging 3 kg block. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the table and the block is 0.2. What is the acceleration of the blocks?

options.why: Correct. Net force (m₂g − μm₁g) divided by the total mass.
Include friction on the table block.
Friction opposes the motion.
Both blocks accelerate; divide by the total mass.

questions.stem: A mass on a spring oscillates with angular frequency 6 rad/s and amplitude 0.05 m. What is its speed when it is 0.035 m from equilibrium?

options.why: Correct. v = ω√(A² − x²), from conservation of energy.
Speed is greatest at equilibrium, not at the ends.
That is the maximum speed, at x = 0.
Use A² − x² under a square root.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a horizontal ledge 7.5 m high at 12 m/s. How far from the base of the ledge does it land?

options.why: Correct. Fall time from the height, times the horizontal speed.
Fall time is √(2h/g).
Take the square root for the time.
Horizontal and vertical motion are independent.

questions.stem: A force $$F(x) = 1x^3$$ N acts along the x-axis. How much work does it do on an object moving from $$x = 2$$ m to $$x = 4$$ m?

options.why: Integrate; do not just evaluate F.
Correct. W = ∫F dx.
The force is not constant.
Divide by n + 1 when integrating.

questions.stem: A curve of radius 120 m is banked so that a car at 15 m/s needs no friction. What is the banking angle?

options.why: Square the speed.
Use tan θ = v²/(rg), from dividing the force components.
Measure the angle from the horizontal.
Correct. tan θ = v²/(rg).

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and slides 6 m down a 37° incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.1. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Correct. mgh − μmg cos θ·L = ½mv².
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
Friction removes energy.
Use the vertical drop, L sin θ.

questions.stem: A 1 kg ball moving at +9 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 5 kg ball at rest. What is the velocity of the 5 kg ball afterward (positive in the original direction)?

options.why: Only equal masses exchange velocities.
Kinetic energy is conserved too.
That would be a sticking collision.
Correct. Elastic: conserve momentum and kinetic energy (relative velocity reverses).

questions.explanation: v₁' = (m₁ − m₂)v/(m₁ + m₂) = -6 m/s; v₂' = 2m₁v/(m₁ + m₂) = 3 m/s.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 7 kg and radius 0.5 m spins at 10 rad/s on a frictionless axle. A 1.25 kg lump of clay is dropped onto the rim and sticks. What is the new angular speed?

options.why: The clay's inertia is mR².
Correct. Angular momentum is conserved: I_iω_i = I_fω_f.
Use rotational inertias, not masses.
Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision.

questions.stem: A block slides down a 35° incline. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.1. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?

options.why: Correct. a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ).
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
The component along the incline is mg sin θ.
Friction acts up the slope.

questions.stem: Two springs with constants 30 N/m and 60 N/m are connected in parallel and support a 0.5 kg mass at rest. How far do they stretch in total?

options.why: The force is the weight, mg.
Correct. k_eq = k₁ + k₂.
Series and parallel rules are reversed.
Both springs share the load.

questions.stem: A 1000 kg car heading east at 19 m/s collides with a 3000 kg car heading north at 17 m/s, and they lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?

options.why: Divide by the total mass.
Momentum is a vector; add components at right angles.
Weight each velocity by its mass.
Correct. Conserve momentum in x and y separately, then combine.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 7 kg and radius 0.5 m rotates about an axis perpendicular to it, 0.5 m from its center. What is its rotational inertia?

options.why: Include the disk's own I about its center.
Correct. Parallel-axis theorem: I = ½MR² + Md².
The axis is not through the center.
The parallel-axis term is Md².

questions.stem: A planet has mass $$3 \times 10^{23}$$ kg and radius $$3 \times 10^{7}$$ m. What is the escape speed from its surface? ($$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$$ N·m²/kg²)

options.why: Correct. ½mv² = GMm/R.
Take the square root.
Potential energy uses 1/R.
That is the circular orbit speed; escape needs √2 times more.

questions.stem: A solid sphere rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of height 3.2 m. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: That is only correct for a hoop.
Correct. mgh = ½mv²(1 + β) with I = ⅖MR².
Some energy goes into rotation.
Rotational energy is ½Iω² = ½βmv².

questions.stem: A system obeys $$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -4x$$. What is the period of its motion?

options.why: T = 2π/ω, not 2πω.
ω is the square root of the coefficient.
Correct. ω = √4 = 2 rad/s, T = 2π/ω.
T = 2π/ω.

questions.stem: An object of mass 0.7 kg falls from rest with a drag force $$F = -bv$$, where $$b = 0.06$$ kg/s. What is its terminal speed?

options.why: That is the time constant.
Drag here is linear in v.
Solve mg = bv for v.
Correct. At terminal speed, mg = bv.

questions.explanation: v_T = mg/b = 114 m/s and τ = m/b = 11.7 s.

questions.stem: A 1.5 kg ball on a 0.4 m string moves in a vertical circle. At the bottom of the circle its speed is 7 m/s. What is the tension in the string there?

options.why: Include gravity.
Correct. At the bottom, T − mg = mv²/r.
Centripetal force uses v².
Check the direction of gravity relative to the center.

questions.stem: A planet has mass $$6 \times 10^{25}$$ kg and radius $$9 \times 10^{6}$$ m. What is the escape speed from its surface? ($$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$$ N·m²/kg²)

options.why: Potential energy uses 1/R.
Take the square root.
That is the circular orbit speed; escape needs √2 times more.
Correct. ½mv² = GMm/R.

questions.stem: An object's acceleration is $$a(t) = 4t$$ m/s². At $$t = 0$$ it has velocity 6 m/s and is at $$x = 0$$. What is its velocity at $$t = 3$$ s?

options.why: Correct. Integrate a(t) and add the initial velocity.
That is the position.
Include the initial velocity.
Integrating tⁿ divides by n + 1.

questions.stem: A 3 kg mass hangs from a light string wrapped around a uniform disk pulley of mass 2 kg that turns on a frictionless axle. What is the acceleration of the mass?

options.why: The pulley's inertia reduces the acceleration.
Correct. a = mg/(m + M/2), using I = ½MR² and a = Rα.
For a disk, I/R² = M/2.
I/R² = M/2.

questions.explanation: mg − T = ma and TR = ½MR²(a/R) give a = 7.35 m/s².

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 0.4 m is pivoted at one end and released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its angular acceleration just after release?

options.why: Use τ = Iα with I = ML²/3.
Correct. τ = Mg(L/2) and I = ML²/3 give α = 3g/(2L).
The weight acts at L/2.
τ = MgL/2.

questions.stem: The potential energy of a particle is $$U(x) = 3x^3 - 6x$$ J. At what positive x is the particle in stable equilibrium?

options.why: Take the square root.
Set the derivative, not U, to zero.
Correct. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0; stable at a minimum.
dU/dx = 3ax² − b.

questions.explanation: dU/dx = 9x² − 6 = 0 gives x = 0.816 m; d²U/dx² > 0 there, so it is stable.

questions.stem: A uniform 8 m beam weighing 200 N rests on supports at both ends. A 500 N load sits 6 m from the left end. What force does the right support exert?

options.why: That is the left support's force.
The load is not at the center.
Include the beam's weight at its center.
Correct. Take torques about the left support.

questions.stem: A 6 kg object at rest experiences a net force $$F(t) = 3t$$ N from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 3$$ s. What is its final speed?

options.why: Divide by the mass to get speed.
Integrate the force over time.
The force is not constant.
Correct. Impulse ∫F dt equals the change in momentum.

questions.stem: Satellite B orbits a planet in a circular orbit 3 times the radius of satellite A's circular orbit. What is the ratio of B's orbital period to A's?

options.why: T² ∝ r³.
Kepler's third law: T ∝ r^(3/2).
The exponent is 3/2.
Correct. T² ∝ r³, so T ∝ r^(3/2).

questions.stem: A 29 g bullet moving at 370 m/s embeds in a 4.9 kg block hanging from strings. How high does the block rise?

options.why: Correct. Momentum for the collision, then energy for the swing.
h = V²/(2g).
Find the block's speed after the collision first.
Kinetic energy is not conserved in the collision.

questions.explanation: V = 2.18 m/s after the collision; h = V²/(2g) = 0.242 m.

questions.title: Block on an incline with a hanging mass

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a free-body diagram for the 6 kg block, labeling each force.

rubric.criterion: Weight down, normal force perpendicular to the incline, tension up the incline.
Kinetic friction down the incline (opposite the motion).

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the acceleration of the system in terms of the masses, θ, μ and g, then calculate its value.

rubric.criterion: Newton's second law applied to each block (or the system).

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the string.
Calculate the speed of the blocks after the hanging block has descended 1.5 m, and the work done by friction on the incline block during that motion.

rubric.criterion: Work by friction, with a negative sign.

parts.prompt: Sketch (describe) graphs of position, velocity and acceleration versus time for one period, aligned vertically.

rubric.criterion: Position is a cosine starting at +A; velocity is a negative sine starting at 0.
rubric.example: x starts at 0.07 m; v starts at 0 and goes negative.

rubric.criterion: Acceleration starts at its negative maximum and is opposite in sign to position throughout.

parts.prompt: Derive expressions for v(t) and a(t), and determine the maximum speed and maximum acceleration.
Calculate the spring constant and the period.
Calculate the total mechanical energy and describe how kinetic and potential energy vary during one period.

rubric.example: K is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A; U is the reverse; the sum is constant. Each varies twice per period.

parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the students could use to measure the period accurately, including how to reduce uncertainty.

rubric.example: Time 10 swings with a stopwatch and divide by 10.

rubric.criterion: Keep the amplitude small and repeat trials.
rubric.example: Release from under about 10° and average several trials.

parts.prompt: Identify quantities to graph that would give a straight line, and explain how g can be found from the graph.
Plot (describe) the linearized data and draw a best-fit line. Use it to calculate an experimental value of g.
The students repeat the experiment with a much larger amplitude. Predict how the measured periods would change and explain.

rubric.criterion: Periods increase slightly; the small-angle approximation (sin θ ≈ θ) no longer holds.
rubric.example: The restoring torque is less than proportional to θ at large angles.

parts.prompt: Without calculating, predict which object reaches the bottom first. Justify your prediction using energy.

rubric.example: It has the smaller rotational inertia per MR².

rubric.criterion: Justification: less of its energy goes into rotation, so more is translational kinetic energy.

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed at the bottom of an object with rotational inertia βMR², in terms of g, h and β.

rubric.criterion: Energy conservation including both forms of kinetic energy, with v = Rω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of each object at the bottom.

rubric.example: solid sphere: 4.27 m/s; solid cylinder: 4.12 m/s

parts.prompt: Explain whether your derived expression is consistent with your prediction in part (a), and why neither speed depends on M or R.

rubric.criterion: Smaller β gives larger v, consistent with the prediction.
M and R cancel in the energy equation.
rubric.example: Only the shape factor β matters.
